issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must permit additional evidence in an appeal against conviction when the evidence is necessary to decide the appeal and its exclusion risks a failure of justice.
material_facts: The accused appealed a conviction for cheating in connection with proposed sales of land held by a trust.

The trial record contained a photocopy of a trust deed, but the trial court did not consider it because it had not been proved; a related resolution authorising steps toward sale also had not been proved.
The trust deed and resolution were relevant to the basis for initiating the sale process and to assessing the accused’s intent.
The accused sought to place certified copies of the documents on the appellate record and to call a witness to prove them.
In a related prosecution arising from the same allegations and transaction, the trust deed and resolution were proved and the accused was acquitted.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court erred in rejecting the applications under Section 391 Cr.P.C. It must receive the trust deed and resolution and permit the accused to lead oral evidence, including at least one witness, to prove the contents of the deed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 391(1) Cr.P.C. empowers an appellate court to take or direct additional evidence when it is necessary for deciding the appeal. Read with the appellate court’s powers under Section 386(b) Cr.P.C., the power is broad and must be exercised to secure justice; necessity is not confined to cases where judgment would otherwise be impossible, but includes cases where exclusion would risk a failure of justice. There is no fixed formula for necessity, and the power must be exercised sparingly and not as a disguise for retrial or to cause prejudice. Rajeswar Prasad Misra v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1965 SC 1887, and Rambhau v. State of Maharashtra, (2001) 4 SCC 759, apply these principles.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The person seeking to adduce evidence is pursuing an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.proposed_evidence_material_to_deciding_a: The proposed evidence bears on an issue the appellate court must decide.
predicates.existing_record_contains_only_unproved_c: The existing record contains only an unproved copy of a document relevant to the appeal.
predicates.proposed_documents_explain_basis_of_tran: The proposed documents explain the basis on which the transaction at the centre of the prosecution was initiated.
predicates.exclusion_would_leave_material_issue_une: Without the proposed evidence, a material issue in assessing the accused’s conduct or intent would remain unexamined.

issues.definition: When a person appealing a criminal conviction offers material documents that explain the transaction and are not proved by the existing record, the appellate court must receive the evidence if excluding it would leave a material issue unexamined.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court must intervene under its inherent jurisdiction when an appellate court wrongly refuses material additional evidence and the stated grounds of delay or bad faith lack support in the record.
material_facts: The accused challenged the appellate court’s refusal of additional evidence by applying to the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
The conviction had been followed by an appeal filed the next day, and the record did not indicate that the appeal was already being heard when the applications for additional evidence were made.
The High Court rejected the challenge on the grounds that the applications were belated and appeared intended to delay the appeal or were motivated by bad faith.
The proposed documents were relevant to the appeal, had been referred to in the trial judgment, and had not been considered because they were unproved.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in refusing to exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. The refusal orders were set aside and the applications for additional evidence were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 482 Cr.P.C. preserves the High Court’s inherent power to secure the ends of justice. Where an appellate court has wrongly refused evidence material to deciding an appeal, unsupported assumptions of delay or bad faith do not justify the High Court’s refusal to intervene. The principles governing additional evidence under Section 391 Cr.P.C., as stated in Rajeswar Prasad Misra v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1965 SC 1887, and Rambhau v. State of Maharashtra, (2001) 4 SCC 759, inform that assessment.

predicates.inherent_jurisdiction_challenge_to_evide: A party asks a High Court to use its inherent jurisdiction to review an appellate court’s refusal to receive evidence.
predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The underlying proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.proposed_evidence_material_to_deciding_a: The evidence sought to be introduced bears on an issue the appellate court must decide.
predicates.refusal_left_material_evidence_unproved: The appellate court’s refusal leaves relevant evidence unproved and unavailable for consideration in the appeal.
predicates.record_does_not_support_delay_or_bad_fai: The record does not support the claim that the application was made to delay the appeal or for a bad-faith purpose.

issues.definition: When a High Court is asked to review an evidentiary refusal in a criminal appeal, it must intervene if the refusal leaves material evidence unproved and the record does not support the asserted grounds of delay or bad faith.
